params.text:
High-quality chest compressions

Chest compressions keep a trickle of oxygen-rich blood moving to the brain and heart, so their quality matters enormously. Get these things right:

  • Position: kneel beside the person and place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest (on the lower half of the breastbone). Place your other hand on top and interlock your fingers.
  • Posture: keep your arms straight and your shoulders directly above your hands, using your body weight to press down.
  • Depth: press down 5–6 cm — at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, roughly a third of the depth of the chest.
  • Rate: compress at a rate of 100–120 per minute.
  • Recoil: allow the chest to come back up fully after each compression — let it recoil completely and do not lean on the chest between compressions.
  • Rescue breaths: if you are trained and willing, combine compressions with rescue breaths in a ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

Keep interruptions to a minimum: every pause lets the blood flow drop away, so make any stop as short as you possibly can.

Sharing the effort as a team

Good CPR is genuinely tiring, and tired rescuers push more shallowly and slowly without realising it. Whenever a second trained person is available, share the work.

  • Swap roughly every two minutes: change over before fatigue sets in, as tired rescuers push less effectively.
  • Keep pauses tiny: plan the swap so compressions stop for barely a second.
  • Coach each other: count out loud and give honest feedback on depth and rate.
  • Take turns with the AED: one person can fetch and set it up while the other keeps compressing.

Working smoothly as a team keeps compressions strong from the very first minute until the ambulance crew take over.

params.textField: Place your hands in the *centre* of the chest. Compress to a depth of *5-6* centimetres, at a rate of *100-120* per minute. Allow the chest to fully *recoil* after each push. Keep *interruptions* to a minimum and swap rescuer every *two* minutes.

params.question: You and a colleague are giving CPR. After a couple of minutes you feel your compressions getting shallower and slower. What is the best action?

answers.text: Swap over quickly with your colleague, keeping any pause in compressions as short as possible.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Swapping about every two minutes keeps compressions strong, and a slick change-over avoids a long, harmful pause.

answers.text: Carry on alone until the ambulance arrives so the count is not lost.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Pushing on while tired means shallow, slow compressions; sharing the effort keeps quality high.

answers.text: Stop CPR completely for a minute to rest, then start again.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A long pause lets blood flow to the brain collapse; you should swap over rather than stop.

answers.text: Push faster than 120 a minute to make up for being tired.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Going faster than 120 reduces the depth and effectiveness of each compression; swap instead.
